input: Given question: What does it mean by isovolumetric contraction of the heart? Option A: This is when the ventricles contracts for the first 0.02-0.03s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the atrioventricular valves are closed and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is little shortening of muscle fibers but there is a decrease in volume. Option B: This is when the atrium contracts for the first 0.02-0.03s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the atrioventricular valves are open and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is no shortening of muscle fibers and the volume does not decrease. Option C: This is when the atrium contracts for the first 0.02-0.05s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the atrioventricular valves are closed and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is little shortening of muscle fibers and there is no emptying. Option D: This is when the ventricles contracts for the first 0.02-0.05s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the semilunar valves are open and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is no shortening of muscle fibers but emptying happens. Option E: This is when the ventricles contracts for the first 0.02-0.03s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the semilunar valves are closed and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is little shortening of muscle fibers and there is no emptying. The correct answer is Option E.
reference: Answer = E - Isovolumetric contractionThis is when the ventricles contracts for the first 0.02-0.03s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the semilunar valves are closed and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is little shortening of muscle fibers and there is no emptying. Atrial contraction (options A & B) refers to the initial phase of ventricular contraction where the atria contract first before the ventricles. However, atrial contraction is part of ventricular systole and is not a separate phase. Semilunar valve opening and closing (options C & D) occurs during ventricular diastole, not systole. During ventricular systole, the semilunar valves are closed. During ventricular diastole, the semilunar valves open, allowing blood to flow back into the atria. Therefore, option C & D are incorrect. http://geekymedics.com/aortic-stenosis-vs-mitral-regurgitation/https://open.oregonstate.education/hcs_641/chapter/17-1-02-a/https://www.cvphysiology.com/Heart%20Disease/HD009c.htmhttps://www.cvphysiology.com/Heart%20Disease/HD009b.htmhttps://www.cvphysiology.com/Heart%20Disease/HD009a.htmhttps://www.cvphysiology.com/Heart%20Disease/HD010.htm
best_explanation: Isovolumetransport describes the initial phase of systole when the ventricles contract for the first 0.02-0.03s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the atrioventricular valves are closed and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is little shortening of muscle fibers and there is no emptying. This is also known as the "ventricular isovolumetric contraction" or "ejection phase". Once the stop codon has been reached, the protein chain is released and the ribosome moves along the mRNA to discard the remaining shuttle. input: Given question: In the production of prostaglandins, the most widely used fatty acid precursor called arachidonic acid must be made. For this to happen, the fatty acid must be cleaved from the membrane phospholipids through the action of an enzyme.What is the name of this enzyme? Option A: Phospholipase B2 - PLB2 Option B: Phospholipase B1 - PLB1 Option C: Phospholipase C Option D: Phospholipase A2 - PLA2 Option E: Phospholipase A1 - PLA1 The correct answer is Option D.
reference: A = incorrect - PLB2 is an enzyme involved in the breakdown of membrane phospholipids of the neuron, to release unsaturated fatty acids, mainly AA, for the synthesis of prostaglandins, and other eicosanoids. B = incorrect - PLB1 is an enzyme involved in the breakdown of membrane phospholipids of the neuron, to release unsaturated fatty acids, mainly AA, for the synthesis of prostaglandins, and other eicosanoids. C = incorrect - Phospholipase C is a general term for two different but related enzymes: one that breaks down phosphatidylcholine to produce IP3 and diacylglycerol, and another that catalyses the opposite process, using a different substrate, to produce ATP and phosphatidylinositol.D = CORRECT - Phospholipase A2 is the specific enzyme which breaks down phosphatidylcholine to produce IP3 and arachidonic acid.E = incorrect - Phospholipase A1 is an enzyme that hydrolyses stored triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol. It is also sometimes calledlipoprotein lipase, as it is able to hydrolyse large triacylglycerol molecules to smaller ones. This enzyme is found in adipose tissue and is released when glucagon stimulates the liver. It hydrolyses the triglyceride stores in adipose tissue, and can therefore increase the availability of free fatty acids for beta-oxidation.This enzyme is produced by the group of cells known as adipocytes. Deficiency of this enzyme results in an inability to control the level of free fatty acids and hence may contribute to obesity. Excess is found in patients with diabetes. This was covered in the plenary on Lipids (Digestion, Absorption, Storage and Metabolism) in Case 6. https://teachmephysiology.com/biochemistry/lipids/prostaglandins/
best_explanation: Phospholipase A2 - PLA2  is the enzyme responsible for cleaving arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids.  Phospholipase B1 - PLB1  is an enzyme that cleaves membrane phospholipids to form IP3 and diacylglycerol.  Phospholipase C  is activated by Gq subunit of a G protein and cleaves PI(4,5)P2 to IP3 and diacylglycerol.  Phospholipase A1 - PLA1  is an enzyme that hydrolyses stored TAG to form FFA and water.  Phospholipase B2 - PLB2  an enzyme that hydrolyses stored TAG to form IP3 and diacylglycerol.  Phospholipase A2 - PLA2  is the correct answer. It is the enzyme responsible for cleaving arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids.  The process of making prostaglandins is as follows: 1. Arachidonic acid is cleaved from phospholipids by phospholipase A2. 2. Arachidonic acid is then taken up by adjacent cells via diffusion. 3. In the second cell, arachidonic acid is brought to the plasma membrane. 4. Arachidonic acid is then hydrolysed to form prostaglandin H2 by phospholipase A2. 5. Prostaglandin H2 is then transported into the nucleus of the cell where it acts as a transcription factor, regulating the expression of specific genes. 6. The effects of prostaglandin H2 act on the local area where the cell is, e.g. causing contraction of smooth muscle.  Prostaglandins take part in many processes within the body, including the regulation of blood pressure and the contraction of uterine muscles. Prostaglandins have a role in many disease states, for example, they are implicated in the formation of blood clots, and are reduced by aspirin. input: Given question: Your GI consultant presents to you a patient that has developed some Gastric ulcers. She tells you that they have ruled out the chances of a H.Pylori cause. The patient is of relatively normal weight and about 30, with no smoking history or alcohol misuse. Before you take a history, the consultant tells you that it is likely another extremely common cause of gastric ulcers, being... Option A: A Gastro-carcinoma Option B: Gastric Neoplasia Option C: Stress Option D: Crohn's Disease Option E: NSAIDS The correct answer is Option E.
reference: 80% of gastric ulcers are caused by NSAID use. NSAIDS inhibit prostaglandin production, which in turn reduces the secretion of bicarbonate and mucus from the stomach. This makes the stomach more susceptible to the effects of acid. 10% are caused by Helicobacter Pylori 5% are caused by Gastro-carcinoma 4% are caused by stress 1% are caused by Crohn's disease (this is very rare) I got this information from the Upper GI case 6 planery lecture from Case 6. If anyone wants to know more about this topic, I highly recommend going to see Alan Watson (the lead GI consultant) he is absolutely fantastic at explaining things. Also, if you don't believe me, feel free to fact check this info on jeff allen's upper gi case 7 powerpoint. I hope this helps! Let me know if you need any more information.
best_explanation: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are a very common cause of gastric ulcers.  The two ways in which they can cause ulcers are:  - Direct damage to the epithelium of the stomach as they pass through it.  - Inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis. Prostaglandins normally protect the stomach from the HCL.  Without them, the HCL in the stomach can cause ulcers. A- Can cause ulcers, but usually with concurrent use of PPIs and H2 receptor antagonistsB- Can cause ulcers as well, but usually with concurrent use of PPIsC- Stress can cause gastric ulcers as well, but usually with concurrent use of PPIsD- Crohn's disease can cause gastric ulcers as well, but usually with concurrent use of PPIs E- Correct. Can cause ulcers as well, but usually with concurrent use of PPIs and H2 receptor antagonists. (From Case 6 Anatomy Lightbulb)  If none of these are the cause, then it is likely to be a H.Pylori infection.  For further information, I found this video very helpful: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2JGK2l1RMV8&t=226s (From 22.20 onwards)  Also, this website has a lot of information on the topic: https://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/gastric-ulcers-treatment (The 'causes' section has a lot of information)  I hope this helps! Let me know if you have any questions.

input: Given question: Poor James, a 5 year old boy, is brought to the GP by his mum who is concerned that he always seems more out of breath than the other children during sport and is often wheezy. You decide that the most likely diagnosis is asthma and prescribe Salbutamol. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of salbutamol? Option A: Beta-2-adrenoreceptor agonist Binds to beta-2-adrenoreceptors which are GPCRThis up regulates adenylate cyclasecAMP increases and activates protein kinase APKA switches of myosin light chain kinase Bronchial smooth muscle relaxes Option B: M3 receptor antagonist Binds to M3 which is a GPCR and blocks acetylcholine from binding This decreases cGMP production cGMP usually causes bronchial smooth muscle contractionLess cGMP causes bronchial smooth muscle relaxation Option C: M3 receptor agonist Binds to M3 which is a GPCR and blocks acetylcholine from bindingThis decreases cGMP productioncGMP usually causes bronchial smooth muscle contractionLess cGMP causes bronchial smooth muscle relaxation Option D: Beta-2-adrenoreceptor antagonistBinds to beta-2-adrenoreceptors which are GPCRThis up regulates adenylate cyclasecAMP increases and activates protein kinase APKA switches of myosin light chain kinaseBronchial smooth muscle relaxes Option E: Inhaled corticosteroid Binds to a glucocorticoid receptor Up regulates transcription anti-inflammatory mediatorsDown regulates transcription of inflammatory mediators Reduces inflammation The correct answer is Option A.
reference: The correct answer is A  Salbutamol is a sympathomimetic drug aka it mimics the sympathetic system effects. It acts on the beta-2-adrenoreceptor in the bronchioles and causes smooth muscle relaxation which widens the airways and reduces inflammation. This is opposite to salmeterol (inhaled anti-asthma drug) which acts on the beta-2-adrenoreceptor in the trachea and causes bronchodilation (widening of the airways) by causing mucus secretion and reducing inflammation. I found this website really helpful for explaining the mechanism of action of different types of asthma drugs http://www.asthma.org.uk/advice/treatment/drugs/long-acting-relievers/salmeterol-fluticasone/why-they-work#:~:text=The%20drug%20is%20absorbed%20into,causes%20bronchodilation%20by%20causing%20mucus%20secretion.&text=Salmeterol%20and%20fluticasone%20both,reduce%20inflammation%20in%20the%20airways.  I also found this video helpful as it explains the mechanism of action of salbutamol and how it differs from salmeterol https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tTgF9IH1fP8&t=466s (the explanation starts at 5:27)  Please note that I am not medically trained and this is all based on my own research, so please do not rely solely on this for your assessments.
best_explanation:
The correct answer is A  Salbutamol is a sympathomimetic drug aka it mimics the sympathetic system effects. It acts on the beta-2-adrenoreceptor in the bronchioles and causes smooth muscle relaxation which widens the airways and reduces inflammation. This is opposed to salmeterol (inhaled anti-asthma drug) which acts on the beta-2-adrenoreceptor in the trachea and upper bronchi to cause coughing to expel mucus. Surgery is usually required if there is evidence of damage to the spermatic cord or the testicular artery has been occluded for more than 8 hours. Most males who experience testicular torsion will regain normal testicular function, but the likelihood of this decreases with increasing duration of ischemia. Testicular torsion can cause permanent damage if blood flow to the testicle is cut off for more than 4 hours. This is because without blood flow, the testicle will begin to die and can no longer produce sperm. After 4 hours, the testicle will have suffered irreversible damage. Treatment includes immediate surgery to untwist the spermatic cord, if this is not possible then the testicle may need to be removed.  Undescended testes- when the testes fail to descend from the abdomen into the scrotum. This condition is also called "cryptorchidism." It's a congenital condition that affects 3-6 percent of full-term males and up to 30 percent of preterm males. It's more common in premature males and males with a family history of the condition. An enlargement of the veins within the scrotum- Hydrocele. Hydrocele is a build-up of fluid in the scrotum due to a blockage of the veins that drain the testicles. The cause of this is not known. It's more common in males who have had testicular torsion or other conditions that cause damage to the testicles or the spermatic cord.  A type of swelling in the scrotum that occurs when fluid collects in the thin sheath surrounding a testicle - this is called a spermatocele.  Diminished functional activity of the gonads due to lower hormone levels- this is hypogonadism.  I hope this helps. Let me know if you have any other questions. Rate highly for more Q&A sessions.  Thank you.

input: Given question: Joints have a rich nerve supply provided by articular nerves. Hilton's law states that the nerves supplying a joint also supply the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering their distal attachments. The nerve of a joint transmits impulses which play a key role in which sense? Option A: Nociception Option B: Proprioception Option C: Exteroception Option D: Interoception Option E: Kinesthesia The correct answer is Option B.
reference:
Hilton’s Law states that the nerves supplying a joint also supply the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering their distal attachments. This means that the nerve of a joint transmits impulses which are related to proprioception. Proprioception is the sense of where your body is in space and time. It allows you to close your eyes and still move your limbs without bumping into things. It is mediated by articular nerves.  Nociception is the sensation of pain. It is mediated by A-delta fibres which are slow (10-20m/s) conducting fibres. They transmit signals of intense pain, often from damaged tissues.  Exteroception is the sensory system concerned with our awareness of stimuli in the environment, such as light touch, vibration, pressure etc. It is mediated by free nerve endings, which are found in the skin.  Interoception refers to the conscious perception of physiological responses or bodily feelings, such as hunger, thirst, fatigue or discomfort. It is not well understood, but it may involve afferent neurons that do not synapse in the spinal cord, but rather in the brain stem or higher brain regions.  Kinesthesia refers to the awareness of the movement of your own body. It is proprioception over longer periods, and so includes the ability to learn and remember motor skills. input: Given question: A patient has been rushed into the emergency ER after suffering a stroke. The neurologist discovers they have lesions in the left S1 and S2 cortices of the brain. When the patient wakes up, the doctor runs some tests including a test that involves pinching the patient. The doctor finds that the patient is experiencing less pain on the right side of the body and struggles to identify the location where they were pinched. Why is this? Option A: The stroke has led to damage of the spinothalamic tract Option B: The stroke has led to damage of the lateral pain system Option C: The patient has a lower perception of pain Option D: The stroke has led to damage medial pain system Option E: The stroke has led to damage of the dorsal column medial leminiscus tract The correct answer is Option B.
reference: Stroke has led to damage of the lateral pain system (which explains why the patient experiences less pain) as well as damage of the spinothalamic tract (which explains why the patient cannot identify where they were pinched). This was taken from the Case 5 plenary on PCS3. I apologise if this seems like a silly question but it took me a while to understand this concept so I thought it would be helpful to create a question around it. Let me know if you need any more information! :) p.s sorry about the long answer!
best_explanation: Stroke has led to damage of the lateral pain system - this system is responsible for the conscious, subjective experience of pain. It is contralateral - i.e. it causes pain on the same side of the body as the lesion.  The spinothalamic tract is part of the dorsal column medial lemniscus tract - this system is responsible for the sensory aspect of pain (thoroughheading, temperature etc) but NOT the conscious experience of pain.  The medial pain system is responsible for the conscious, subjective experience of pain but it is ipsilateral - i.e. it causes pain on the same side of the lesion as the lesion.  The patient may also have a lower perception of pain due to the stroke but this is not the main reason for the neurologist's observations.  The patient struggles to identify the location of the pinch as the lesion has led to a disconnection between sensory and motor areas of the brain.  The patient is left with a sensory loss on the right side of the body but can still feel pain.  The patient cannot identify the location of the pinch as the sensory and motor areas of the brain are disconnected.  This was taken from the Case 5 PCS3 lecture.  I hope this helps. input: Given question: Hypertension can be defined as persistent blood pressure greater than or equal to 140/90mmHg. There are many antihypertensive drugs including one called Losartan. reference: Losartan is an angiotensin II receptor blocker so it works by preventing the action of angiotensin II. E- Thiazide like diuretics such as Chlorothiazide remove excess salt from the body via the kidneys, this reduces blood viscosity and therefore blood pressure. input: Given question: What would happen if a child had growth hormone in excess? Option A: Acromegaly Option B: Gigantism Option C: Dwarfism Option D: No effect The correct answer is Option B.
reference: If a child has growth hormone in excess they will develop gigantism. This means that the bones will grow faster than usual resulting in tall stature. However due to the fact that the epiphyseal plates are still open, the bones will continue to grow in length. In adults this condition is called acromegaly. It is caused by a pituitary tumour and results in tall stature and various other symptoms such as excessive sweating and diabetes.  Growth hormone deficiency in children will result in dwarfism. This is because there is an insufficient amount of growth hormone to stimulate the production of IGF-1 which in turn prevents the development of the bones and results in short stature. In adults it is called hypopituitarianism. It may be caused by damage to the pituitary gland, hypothyroidism or a tumour that affects the pituitary gland. There will be no effect on the body if there is an even amount of growth hormone. This is because growth hormone works on a pinpoint basis. It only affects the cells in its immediate area. Therefore if there is an even amount of growth hormone in the body there will be no noticeable effect. This was taken from the PCS 3 lecture on growth hormone. best_explanation:
If a child has growth hormone in excess they will have gigantism.  Gigantism is excessive growth and result from childhood to adulthood. It is caused by a tumour of the pituitary gland or by abnormal growth of the cells that form the pituitary gland, resulting in excess production of growth hormone.  The excess growth hormone causes the bones to grow faster, resulting in gigantism.  Acromegaly is the effect of excess growth hormone in adults. reference:
This is a fall on an outstretched hand, therefore there is a high likelihood of scaphoid fracture. Symptoms include pain in the anatomical snuffbox (located immediately proximal to the lateral carpal bones) and abduction of the ipsilateral shoulder indicates a scaphoid fracture. input: Given question: Paul has a cracking headache, so decides to take some aspirin. Aspirin is a non-competitive inhibitor of PGHS1 and 2 enzymes. In terms of kinetics, how is Vmax, Km and Kcat affected? Option A: Vmax will increaseKm will decreaseKcat will increase Option B: Vmax will decreaseKm will not changeKcat will decrease Option C: Vmax will not change Km will decreaseKcat will increase Option D: Vmax will increaseKm will not changeKcat will decrease Option E: Vmax will increaseKm will decreaseKcat will not change The correct answer is Option B.
reference: From the fact that aspirin is a non-competitive inhibitor, we know that it doesn't matter whether or not the enzyme is saturated with substrate - the inhibition will be the same. Therefore, Vmax will decrease because no matter how much substrate there is, the enzyme activity will be reduced by the presence of aspirin (so the maximum rate of reaction will be lower). Also, Km would decrease because the concentration of substrate that produces half of Vmax (i.e. Km) will be higher due to the presence of aspirin (which lowers Vmax). Finally, since aspirin is not a competitive inhibitor, Kcat will stay the same because the affinity of the enzyme for the substrate is unchanged. I made up all of the other answers - I hope this explanation helps! Let me know if you have any questions. Cheers, Sian.
best_explanation: - Non-competitive inhibitors bind to the enzyme, not to the substrate - In terms of kinetics, Vmax will decrease because maximum rate of reaction has decreased - Km will not change because the substrate concentration does not affect the enzyme-inhibitor complex formation - Kcat will decrease because the enzyme is not saturated with substrate, so cannot catalyse the reaction any faster.  - Competitive inhibitors bind to the substrate, not the enzyme - In terms of kinetics, Vmax will decrease because maximum rate of reaction has decreased - Km will decrease because as more substrate is added, the enzyme-substrate complex formation is greater - Kcat will increase because the enzyme is saturated with substrate, so can catalyse the reaction faster. reference: 2:1 or 3:1 second degree heart block is when not all impulses reach the ventricles, so atrial depolarisation is not synchronised with ventricular depolarisation. there are three types of 2:1 block- Mobitz type 1, Mobitz type 2 and 2:1:1 (also called 2:2:1) Mobitz type 2 is when there is a delay in the conduction of the AV node and sometimes not all P waves are followed by a QRS complex. this means that occasionally (at a rate of about 25%) a QRS complex will be dropped. If the PR interval is prolonged this suggests that less than 10% of the impulses are getting through to depolarise the ventricles. As the RR interval increases, it suggests that more impulses are being conducted from the atria to the ventricles (ie- higher ejection fraction). input: Given question: A patient enters a GP surgery having hit her elbow on a banister whilst walking down the stairs. When making a fist, only her pinky and ring finger are able to bend. What nerve has the patient damaged? Option A: Ulnar Option B: Median Option C: Radial Option D: Musculocutaneous Option E: Axillary The correct answer is Option B.
reference:
https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/nerves/median-nerve/ - check out this website for more information on the median nerve and its functionThe median nerve innervates all of the flexors in the forearm, apart from the flexor carpi ulnaris (which is innervated by the ulnar nerve). Therefore, since the flexors are the only muscles being supplied by the median nerve, if she can't make a fist, it means that the median nerve is damaged. The radial and ulnar nerves both innervatethe extensor muscles in the forearm, so if the patient can't make a fist, it doesn't mean that either of these nerves are damaged. The musculocutaneous nerve does not innervate any of the muscles in the forearm, so it is unlikely that the patient's damage is to this nerve. Finally, the axillary nerve innervates the deltoid and teres minor, neither of which are located in the forearm, so it is unlikely that this nerve is damaged. Overall, the median nerve is the most likely nerve to be damaged, given the symptoms presented.

input: Given question: What is the primary control centre for descending pain modulation? Option A: periaqueductal gray Option B: thalamus Option C: dorsal horn of spinal cord Option D: nucleus raphe magnus Option E: reticular formation The correct answer is Option A.
reference:
Periaqueductal gray (PAG) is the primary control centre for descending pain modulation.The PAG sends descending projections to the dorsal horn and is the final pathway for the modulation of nociceptive sensory information. The PAG can inhibit or facilitate the release of substance P via interneurons that project to the dorsal horn. In this way it can influence the experience of pain.The dorsal horn of the spinal cord is where ascending sensory information from the body's tissues is processed and then sent to the brain for interpretation.The thalamus is the second relay station in the ascending pathways, receiving information from the dorsal horn and transmitting it to the somatosensory homunculus in the cerebral cortex.This information is then interpreted by the brain to determine the quality of the sensation, such as sharp/dull, aching etc.The nucleus raphe magnus is a part of the brainstem involved in the regulation of serotonin.Serotonin is important in the descending pain modulation system as it is a neurotransmitter used by the descending neurones projecting to the dorsal horn.  The reticular formation is a part of the brainstem involved in arousal and consciousness. It is not directly involved in pain modulation. information source; pain management lecture, PCS2 tutorial document, pain and nociception lecture, PCS1 tutorial document. references; McBeth, J. best_explanation: The periaqueductal gray (PAG) is the primary control centre for descending pain modulation. The PAG sends descending influences to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, where it modulates the transmission of pain signals. The PAG can inhibit or facilitate the release of substance P, the neuropeptide that carries the sensation of pain. The PAG can also modulate the release of endogenous opioids, which are natural painkillers. The PAG receives information from various brain regions, including the amygdala, the hypothalamus, and the cingulate cortex. The PAG is also connected to the spinothalamic tract, which carries pain information from the body to the brain.  Thalamus: The thalamus is the second relay station in the pain pathway. Thalamic neurons are the second relay in the pain pathway, and project to the primary and secondary somatosensory cortices in the brain. The somatosensory cortices are concerned with sensory discrimination, and can determine the location, discriminative feature and intensity of the pain. The thalamus can also modulate the incoming pain information by changing the pattern of firing of its neurons.  Dorsal horn of spinal cord: The dorsal horn of the spinal cord is the final receiver of the afferent pathway. Here, the pain information is processed and transmitted to the brain. The dorsal horn is the second relay station in the pain pathway, and here the pain information is transmitted to the brain in the lateral spinothalamic tract.  Nucleus raphe magnus: The nucleus raphe magnus is the brain region that makes serotonin. Serotonin can modulate pain sensitivity by inhibiting the release of substance P.  Reticular formation: The reticular formation is a part of the brainstem, and is concerned with arousal and consciousness. The reticular formation can modulate the transmission of pain information by changing the activity of the spinothalamic tract.  Case 5: Pain: Brain and Behaviour. input: Given question: Emily Davies, a 19-year-old female, comes to A+E after sustaining an injury to her hand and is unable to oppose her thumb but can abduct it, which muscle is likely to be damaged? reference: Opposable thumb muscles -Emily can abduct (move away from midline) but not oppose (make close to midline) her thumb so opponens pollicis is damaged. -Flexor pollicis brevis and flexor digiti minimi brevis are both in the superficial layer of the anterior compartment of the hand and are responsible for flexion of the MCP joints. -Adductor pollicis is in the deep layer of the anterior compartment and is responsible for adduction (bring towards midline) of the thumb. -Abductor pollicis brevis is also in the superficial layer and is responsible for abduction (move away from midline) of the thumb. TIP-opposition vs abduction opposition=the ability to make close to midline in order to use the thumb as a thumb.abduction=the ability to move away from midline. eg if you put your thumb by your side and move it away from your side it's abduction. if you put your thumb by your side and move it closer to your thumb it's opposition.  reference https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/muscles/anterior-compartment/hand/opponens-pollicis/  and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537148/ Deltoid-A muscle located on the posterior side of the upper arm. It is one of the chief muscles of the rotator cuff. The deltoid is a large muscle with two heads (a superior and an inferior head) which are united by a common tendinous belly. The fibers of the deltoid are inserted into the tuberosity of the humerus.The main part of the deltoid muscle is located on the lateral border of the scapula above the teres minor. The deltoid is innervated by the axillary nerve and its main function is to provide stability to the glenohumeral joint and assist in abduction of the arm. Damage to this muscle may occur from a fractured humerus or dislocation of the shoulder. Nerve damage to the axillary nerve may cause weakness and paralysis of the deltoid.https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/muscles/posterior-compartment/deltoid/  and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537148/  LATERAL COLLATORAL LIGAMENT-a band of connective tissue that surrounds and supports the lateral condyle of the humerus. It is attached to the humeral shaft at one end and the greater tubercle of the humerus at the other. Its main part lies beneath the teres minor muscle, and its anterior and posterior margins lie respectively 3 and 3.5 cm lateral to the articular margin of the humeral shaft. The ligament prevents posterior displacement of the humeral head relative to the glenoid. This holds the humeral head tightly in the glenoid, thereby helping to stabilize the shoulder joint. A tear of this ligament is called a shoulder dislocation. A dislocation occurs when the force acting upon the glenohumeral joint is great enough to pull the humeral head from the glenoid. Dislocations generally occur in a forward direction; i.e., the humeral head is forced under the acromion process of the scapular. A dislocation can be reduced manually (by pressing the humeral head back into the glenoid), or surgery may be necessary. After a first-time dislocation, the glenohumeral joint is never truly "stable" again. The risk of future dislocations is always present. The supraspinatus is the most commonly torn muscle in the rotator cuff. It originates from the supraspinous fossa of the scapula above the teres minor and the great tubercle of the humerus. The tendons of the supraspinatus passes beneath the acromion process

It is innervated by the ulnar nerve and its main function is to oppose the thumb.  Flexor pollicis brevis, flexor digiti minimi brevis, and abductor pollicis brevis are all innervated by the median nerve and are all located in the palm of the hand, so are unlikely to be damaged in the injury described.  Adductor pollicis is also located in the palm of the hand, however it is innervated by the ulnar nerve, and its main function is to aid in the abduction of the thumb, not opposition. LOAF = Flexor digitorum profundus (ulnar nerve), opponens pollicis (ulnar nerve), abductor pollicis brevis (median nerve), flexor pollicis brevis (median nerve)  Hence opponens pollicis is the right answer as it is the only muscle innervated by the ulnar nerve and its main function is to oppose the thumb. reference:
ACE-I block the conversion of angiotensin I to II by plasma bradykinin. This prevents the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) from activating. RAAS increases salt and water retention which increases blood pressure. ACE-I are more effective when used with a low dose of a diuretic (water pill). Combining these two drugs removes excess fluid, which reduces blood pressure. ACE-I have few side effects but they can lower the white blood cell count and potentiate the effects of antibiotic. ACE-I are more suitable for people who are allergic to penicillan (penicillin), cephalosporins or sulphonamides. Which one of the following medications is suitable? Option A: Diazepam Option B: Propofol Option C: Amobarbital Option D: Lignocaine Option E: Nitrous oxide The correct answer is Option D.
reference: Lignocaine (or lidocaine) is a amino amide local anaesthetic that inhibits fast-gated sodium channels. It is also used as an antiarrhythmic and as a stabiliser of the neuronal membrane. It is volatile and can be used with nitrous oxide as a vapour. Nitrous oxide is a weak vasodilator and lignocaine is a mild beta adrenoreceptor agonist so their interaction causes a slight decrease in blood pressure. Nitrous oxide has a very short half life and works quickly so is useful for minor surgery. The other options are all central nervous system depressants; diazepam is a benzodiazepine, propofol is a dissociative anaesthetic and amobarbital (also known as Amytal) is a barbiturate. These work by enhancing GABAergic activity. They have a high therapeutic index i.e. it takes a lot to overdose but they have a high risk of addiction and withdrawal symptoms. Nitrous oxide is very safe and has no major side effects or risks when used correctly.  All these drugs can be used as premedication before surgery. However, as fast-gated Na+ channels are also located in cardiac myocytes, the use of these drugs will also stop the heart. So unless there is an emergency, the above drugs cannot be used for this purpose.  I took most of this information from Dr Coffey's pharmacology light bulb. He always says "if it's not funny it's because it's true" so I hope this was helpful! Let me know if you want any more detail on anything :) xxxx

What is the most likely diagnosis and best treatment for the patient? Option A: ACL tear and non-operative therapy program of 6 to 8 weeks Option B: ACL tear and operative therapy program of 6 to 9 months Option C: PCL tear and operative therapy program of 6 to 9 months Option D: PCL tear and non-operative program of 6 to 8 weeks Option E: A stable patella fracture and non-perative therapy program of 6 to 8 weeks The correct answer is Option B.
reference:

This puts huge amounts of stress on the knee joint, and can cause the ACL to rupture. The patient may also have damaged their PCL as well. Root cause: the patient has a mechanical instability of the knee, which causes the ACL to rupture. This can be due to poor technique when changing direction, or a predisposition to valgus (inward) collapse of the knee. This can be improved upon with proper rehabilitation, but may remain a problem throughout the patients life. input: Given question: Neurotransmitters are vital chemicals for communication between neurones and span a variety of responsibilities. Which major class of these chemicals are considered responsible for things like consciousness, attention, cognition and emotion? Option A: Amino acid neurotransmitters Option B: Monoamines Option C: Catecholamines Option D: Peptide neurotransmitters The correct answer is Option B.
reference:
Consciousness, attention, cognition and emotion are all functions of the monoamine neurotransmitters, which include serotonin, histamine, dopamine and norepinephrine. These neurotransmitters act on axons with gaps between their terminal buttons (synapse). This type of synapse is called a chemical synapse. A - Amino acid neurotransmitters are responsible for functions such as stimulating muscles (e.g. acetylcholine), transmitting information through sensory organs (e.g. glutamate) and modulating pain (e.g. endorphins). They act on cells that have receptors embedded in the membrane. B - Catecholamines refer to two monoamines; Dopamine and norepinephrine. Their names come from the fact that they have a benzene ring and a double bond (hence catechol) and that they are amines (NH2). They act on the sympathetic nervous system, being responsible for the fight or flight response. C- Peptide neurotransmitters are made up. D- All neurotransmitters are involved in some way with physiology and behaviour, but some are more 'major' than others. The categories above are not exhaustive, and there are many other classes of neurotransmitter, e.g. hormones (adrenaline, thyroid hormone), local anaesthetics (tetracaine) and neuropeptides (substance P, substance K). It is worth noting that some neurotransmitters can fit into multiple categories; serotonin, for example, is both an amino acid and a monoamine. See the PCS 3 lecture on Chemical Communication for more detail.

reference:
Amnesia can be caused by: - Certain medications - Trauma - Substance abuse - Infections such as herpes - Hypoxia/anoxia - Korsakoff Syndrome - Depression/schizophrenia - Head trauma - Stress - Alzheimer's disease - Stroke  Ageing is not a cause of amnesia, although memory loss is more common in older people due to age related decline in cognitive function.  Link to case 4 auditory pathways lecture: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nkC1vZaUpxs&t=259s (from 13 mins)  Link to case 6 semantic dementia lecture: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S8wWr92Kiqw (from 23 mins)  Link to case 7 stroke lecture: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YHHDJ0TkPXQ (from 21 mins)
==============================================================================================================  This was taken from the case 7 lecture on stroke and is a useful summary of different types of amnesia: There are different types of amnesia depending on what causes it. There are 2 main types: Anterograde – meaning memory loss that affects new memories. This is more common An example would be caused by head trauma or a strokeRetrograde – meaning memory loss that mainly affects old memories. This is less common Examples include; Korsakoff’s syndrome, alcoholic memory loss, herpes simplex virus infection, hypothyroidism, depression, schizophrenia, alzheimers  Another type is temporary amnesia which can be caused by; trauma, stress, seizures, severe emotional distress, oxygen deprivation, ingestion of certain drugs, alcohol withdrawal, sleep disorders, hyperventilation, head injury, hypoglycemia, hyperthyroidism  All these different causes have one thing in common – they cause disruption to short term memory. Memory loss can be either retrograde (prior to illness/injury) or anterograde (after illness/injury). Sometimes there is a reversible cause e.g. vitamin B12 deficiency, thiamine deficiency, hypercalcemia. Sometimes it is irreversible e.g. anoxia/hypoxia, traumatic brain injury, bleeding into the brain/around the brain.  People often confuse dementia with amnesia but they are not the same thing. Dementia is a broader term that describes a decline in cognitive function that is so severe it interferes with daily life. Memory loss is just one symptom of dementia. For example someone may have vascular dementia where they have had a series of mini-strokes which causes memory loss but they may still remember things from before their illness. Whereas with Korsakoff syndrome the patient will have difficulty recalling both recent and past memories.  Case 6 lecture on semantic dementia highlighted how memory loss can be profound yet the person is often aware of this and finds it very distressing. They may know what they want to say but the words aren’t there. It is thought that semantic dementia may be the most common form of early onset dementia. It originates from the sensory cortex and descends through the lateral part of the spinal cord to synapse in the brainstem. It is a bilateral pathway and controls the contralateral muscles. The tectospinal tract is a motor pathway that controls the muscles of the head and neck. It originates from the sensory cortex and descends through the posterior part of the spinal cord to synapse in the brainstem. It is a bilateral pathway and controls the contralateral muscles. input: Given question: A 25 year old women came at the A&I with a fracture at the surgical neck of the humerus. What is the most likely nerve she damaged because of the fracture? Option A: Ulnar nerve Option B: Musculocutanous nerve Option C: Median nerve Option D: Axillary nerve Option E: Long thoracic nerve The correct answer is Option D.
reference:
The axillary nerve passes medially to the surgical neck of the humerus and may be damaged by a fracture at this area. Symptoms of this would include weakness and loss of sensation in the shoulder region. A-Ulnar nerve does not pass close to the surgical neck of the humerusB-Musculocutanous nerve is posterior to the surgical neckC-Symptoms of a fracture at the surgical neck of the humerus would not suggest muscle wasting or colour changes (musculocutanous nerve)D-The axillary nerve passes medially to the surgical neck of the humerus so it is most likely to be damagedE-Long thoracic nerve does not pass close to the surgical neck of the humerus either. This nerve damage will result in paralysis to the serratus anterior muscle which pulls the scapulae outwards. Therefore resulting in a winged scapula. There would also be weakness in the upper arm. Winged Scapula: https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/muscles/back/serratus-anterior/winged-scapula/ (Note the downward pull on the scapulae by the serratus anterior would normally keep the costal surface of the scapulae closely apposed to the ribs. When this muscle is paralysed, the scapulae are no longer held against the ribs, and are instead pulled away from the ribs by the deltoid and trapezius muscles.) https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/injuries/fractures/surgical-neck-fracture/ (The surgical neck is the most common site of fracture of the humerus; it is an area of weakness caused by a narrowing of the bone. Fractures here often occur when falling on an outstretched hand. The ends of the broken bones may push through the skin. It is important to get medical attention immediately if this happens. Surgery may be needed to repair the damage.)
It is important to always consider nerve damage when there is a fracture at the surgical neck of the humerus. The axillary nerve is most likely to be damaged. Damage to this nerve will result in weakness and loss of sensation in the shoulder region. In addition, it may cause paralysis to the deltoid and teres minor muscles. Since these muscles are responsible for abducting the arm past 15 degrees from the midline, this would result in a condition known as "claw hand" where the arm cannot be abducted past 15 degrees from the midline. Furthermore, it may cause a loss of sensation over the regimental badge area. http://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/nerves/axillary/ - This website has great information on the axillary nerve including its function, innervation and possible lesions. input: Given question: What is the mechanism through which nitric oxide (NO) causes vasodilation? Option A: NO activates guanylate cyclase, this causes the conversion of GTP to cGMP. cGMP then activates pKG which phosphorylates myosin light chain kinase, therefore causing vasodilation. Option B: NO activates guanylate cyclase, this causes the conversion of GTP to cGMP. cGMP then activates pKG which leads to the activation of myosin phosphatase which dephosphorylates myosin light chain kinase, therefore causing vasodilation. Option C: NO activates adenyl cyclase, this causes the conversion of ATP to cAMP. cAMP then activates pKA which leads to the activation of myosin phosphatase which dephosphorylates myosin light chain kinase, therefore causing vasodilation. Option D: NO activates adenyl cyclase, this causes the conversion of ATP to cAMP. cAMP then activates pKA  which phosphorylates myosin light chain kinase, therefore causing vasodilation. The correct answer is Option B.
reference: Nitric oxide (NO) activates guanylate cyclase, this causes the conversion of GTP to cGMP. cGMP then activates pKG which leads to the activation of myosin phosphatase which dephosphorylates myosin light chain kinase, therefore causing vasodilation. Myosin light chain kinase phosphorylates myosin light chain which attaches to actin and pulls the sarcomere together, therefore causing contraction. By inhibiting myosin light chain kinase, we are effectively stopping the process of contraction, allowing the vessel to dilate. Option A: prevention of smooth muscle relaxation Option B: trigger smooth muscle releaxation Option C: cause the active contraction of smooth muscle Option D: lead to an increased heart rate Option E: potentially trigger an asthma attack The correct answer is Option B.
reference: β2-adrenoceptors are Gs-coupled receptors that are stimulated by noradrenaline. They are located in many tissues, including in the lungs and the heart. Activation of β2-adrenoceptors usually causes smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation, which reduces the resistance in the lungs, so that air can be inspired more easily (this is why β2-adrenoceptors are also called "bronchodilators"). In the heart, activation of β2-adrenoceptors usually causes negative chronotropic effects, i.e., a reduction of the heart rate. β2-adrenoceptors may also be located in cells of the immune system, where they may function as "off" switches for inflammation. When activated, β2-adrenoceptors downregulate the activity of mast cells and eosinophils, two cell types that are involved in the early phases of an allergic reaction, thereby potentially preventing or dampening an asthma attack.  Answers A and C are therefore incorrect. Answer D is correct, but not entirely accurate, since β2-adrenoceptors are usually "bronchodilators", which means that they cause vasodilation, and hence lower resistance in the lungs, making it easier to breathe. This should lead to a lower heart rate, as the heart does not have to work as hard to oxygenate the body.  Answer E is completely made up. I'm not sure where this information came from, but it is completely wrong. I hope this clears things up! beta 2 receptors are found in smooth muscle and the heart.  binding of an agonist (such as noradrenaline) will lead to smooth muscle relaxation in the airways and potentially trigger an asthma attack  in the heart it will cause the active contraction of smooth muscle (leading to a stronger heart beat)  note that there are also beta 1 receptors in the heart  beta 1 receptors are linked to the sympathetic nervous system  beta 2 receptors are linked to the parasympathetic nervous system  this is a important distinction as beta 1 receptors can be targeted by beta blockers (such as propanolol) to treat angina and high blood pressure  while beta 2 receptors cannot be targeted by beta blockers as they are only found in the heart and not in other areas of the body that need the sympathetic nervous system response (such as the lungs and blood vessels)  I used the following website to form this question: https://teachmephysiology.com/respiratory-system/regulation/neurotransmitters/ - the information on here is quite detailed and easy to understand  I would recommend a quick read if you are struggling with this topic! instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Upon fertilisation what hormone is produced by a developing embryo prior to placenta formation? Option A: Progesterone Option B: Oestrogen Option C: hCG Option D: GNRH The correct answer is Option C.
reference:
During the early stages of development before the placenta forms, it is the developing embryo that produces hCG. This is important as it prevents the mother's immune system from rejecting the developing embryo as foreign tissue. Once the placenta is developed enough to produce progesterone and oestrogen, the developing embryo stops producing hCG. However, hCG can still be detected in the mother's blood because it has crossed the placenta. Later on, when the placenta is fully developed, it is the placenta that produces hCG. hCG is also produced in males to stimulate Leydig cells to produce testosterone  Practical application:   hCG is used in assisted reproduction techniques such as IVF. It can be given to the mother to take orally or can be administered via injection. It is also used to boost low amh levels in women undergoing ivf due to low oestrogen levels. It can also be given to men to boost tesosterone levels if they have low sperm counts.   Reference: Case 6 Anatomy Practical - Reproductive Health
Another useful website is: https://www.fertile-health.info/hcg-injections.html   Extra Info:   When a fertilised egg implants into the uterine lining, it is the placenta that begins to produce hormones such as progesterone and oestrogen. These hormones maintain the endometrium and allow it to thicken to support the developing foetus. After the placenta is formed, the developing embryo (now called a foetus) no longer produces hCG but the placenta continues to do so.  Prior to the development of the placenta, the developing embryo produces hCG to prevent the mother's immune system from rejecting the developing foetus as foreign tissue. This is because the mother's immune system does not yet recognise the developing foetus as a 'self' cell. Instead, it recognises the embryo as a foreign object and would attempt to destroy it. The hCG tricks the mother's immune system into thinking that the developing foetus is indeed a part of her own body and therefore should not be attacked. This was covered in the reproductive anatomy lecture in case 4.  Later on, once the placenta is developed enough, it is the placenta that produces hCG. This is because the placenta has a much greater capacity for producing hormones than the developing embryo. Even though the developing embryo no longer produces hCG, hCG can still be detected in the mother's blood because it has crossed the placenta. This was covered in the reproductive hormones lecture in case 5.  Lastly, hCG is also produced in males to stimulate Leydig cells to produce testosterone. Leydig cells are found in the testicles and are responsible for producing testosterone. If a male has low levels of testosterone, hCG can be administered to stimulate the production of Leydig cells which will then produce testosterone. This was covered in the reproductive hormones lecture in case 5.
best_explanation: Upon fertilisation, prior to the formation of the placenta, the developing embryo produces hCG. This is the hormone that enables the corpus luteum to produce progesterone.  After the placenta is formed, it is the placenta that produces hCG.  If for any reason the corpus luteum fails, the placenta takes over production of hCG.  Oestrogen is produced by the developing embryo after the placenta has formed.  GNRH is produced by the hypothalamus in response to low progesterone and oestrogen. This stimulates the anterior pituitary to produce the gonadotrophins FSH and LH.  Progesterone is produced by the corpus luteum (after the placenta has formed) and the placenta.  Oestrogen is produced by the developing embryo after the placenta has formed and by the placenta.  hCG is produced by the developing embryo prior to the formation of the placenta.  GNRH is produced by the hypothalamus.  FSH and LH are produced by the anterior pituitary.  Progesterone and oestrogen are reproductive hormones.  hCG is a hormone essential for reproduction but is not strictly reproductive.  GNRH and FSH/LH are trophic hormones - they stimulate the anterior pituitary to produce reproductive hormones.  The placenta is a structure that forms in the uterus during pregnancy. It provides a source of nutrients for the foetus and enables the exchange of gases. It also has a number of hormonal functions, including the production of hormones essential for reproduction.  The hypothalamus is a small endocrine gland in the brain that is responsible for producing a number of hormones that regulate homeostasis. It is stimulated by releasing hormones produced by other endocrine glands.  The anterior pituitary is a small endocrine gland located in the anterior (closest to the front) lobe of the hypophysis (the pituitary gland). input: Given question: A young male child is brought into the clinic. His mother says that he bleeds easily and has bleeding joints characterised by stiffness, pain swelling and heat. You suspect haemophilia A and decide to carry out a test for the intrinsic pathway. What test should you carry out ? Option A: PT Option B: APTT Option C: CT Option D: ATP The correct answer is Option B.
reference: APTT would be expected to be very prolonged in haemophilia A as Factor VIII is deficient/missing so the intrinsic pathway is activated and takes much longer to consume the substrate (collagen). This is one of the tests carried out for haemophilia along with a test for factor VIII levels. There is also a test for factor IX levels which would be abnormal in haemophilia B. Haemophilia A & B are X linked recessive disorders. symptoms for haemophilia C are less severe and it is caused by a deficiency/malfunction of factor XIV. Haemophilia A, B & C all result in uncontrolled bleeding. Haemophilia A & B are inherited through a mutation on the X chromosome where as haemophilia C is not inherited but is instead caused by a spontaneous mutation in the gene. refer to dr watson's lecture on haemostasis and blood clotting from case 2. also refer to jeff allen's upper gi case 6 planery cell dysfunction for more detailed information on haemophilia.  http://www.hematology.org.uk/blood-disorders/haemophilia.html  http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/Haemophilia/Pages/Introduction.aspx   http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/haemophilia-types-and-symptoms     http://www.rchsd.org/health-articles/q-a-haemophilia/#:~:text=Haemophilia%20is%20a%20genetic%20disease%2C%20in,activated%20by%20trauma%20or%20infection.&text=A%20defect%20in%20factor%20XII%20means,carried%20out%20to%20determine%20if%20it%20is%20present.%20(APTT)%20test%20will%20be%20prolonged.%20This%20will%20take%20longer%20than%20the%20activated%20by%20trauma%20or%20infection.%20This%20is%20one%20of%20the%20tests%20carried%20out%20for%20haemophilia%20along%20with%20a%20test%20for%20factor%20VIII%20levels.%20There%20is%20also%20a%20test%20for%20factor%20IX%20levels%20which%20would%20be%20abnormal%20in%20haemophilia%20B.%20Haemophilia%20A%20&%20B%20are%20X%20linked%20recessive%20disorders.%20Symptoms%20for%20haemophilia%20C%20are%20less%20severe%20and%20it%20is%20caused%20by%20a%20deficiency%2Fmalfunction%20of%20factor%20XIV.%20Haemophilia%20A,%20B%20&%20C%20all%20result%20in%20uncontrolled%20bleeding.%20Haemophilia%20A%20&%20B%20are%20inherited%20through%20a%20mutation%20on%20the%20X%20chromosome%20whereas%20haemophilia%20C%20is%20not%20inherited%20but%20is%20instead%20caused%20by%20a%20spontaneous%20mutation%20in%20the%20gene.%20refer%20to%20dr%20
best_explanation: APTT would test the intrinsic pathway as it is a test for the activity of Factor 8 which is the first step in the intrinsic pathway. PT would only test for the extrinsic pathway as it is a test for the activity of Factor 11 which is the first step in the extrinsic pathway.  C and D are irrelevant to this question.  Haemophilia A is a disease of the intrinsic pathway as it is a mutation of Factor 8. Haemophilia B is a disease of the extrinsic pathway as it is a mutation of Factor 9. For further information on Haemophilia and the different types, I found the following link very useful : http://www.haemophilia.org.uk/bleeding-disorders/types-haemophilia#.UbM2KNKzYdV#.UbM2KNKzYdV Haemophilia A and B are X linked recessive diseases and are found mainly in males. They are rare diseases. In haemophilia A, there is a deficiency in factor 8 and in haemophilia B there is a deficiency in factor 9. These factors are part of the intrinsic pathway so the clinical symptoms would include easy bleeding and bleeding joints characterised by stiffness, pain, swelling and heat. The genetic defect in haemophilia A and B is on the X chromosome. As males have only one copy of the X chromosome they are more likely to be affected. Females are less likely to be affected as they have two X chromosomes which means one of them is likely to have a normal gene that is not affected. However, in some cases females can be carriers of the disease. There are treatment options available for haemophilia A and B. These include the use of factor 8 and 9 which can be used to top up the levels of these factors in the body. This can be done by injections or by a drip into a vein. Desmopressin is a drug that can be used to increase the levels of factor 8 in the body. This drug is usually only used in mild cases or in conjunction with other treatments. input: Given question: Which of the following acts as an agonist on alpha 1 adrenoceptors? Option A: Salbutamol Option B: Prazosin Option C: Bisoprolol Option D: Timolol Option E: Phenylephrine The correct answer is Option E.
reference:
Alpha 1 Adrenoceptors are found in the heart and act to decrease heart rate and blood pressure.Phenylephrine is an agonist of these receptors and so it has an effect similar to adrenaline. This drug is used to test for alpha 1 adrenoceptor blockade (e.g. to assess if a patient is taking an alpha 1 antagonist drug).  I formed this question based on the pharmacology lightbulb case 2 on the cardiac physiology workshop. For more information on this see the case 2 pharmacology document under the 'drug' tab. Other alpha 1 adrenoceptor blockers include labetalol and carvedilol.Reference: Case 2 pharmacology document under 'drug' tab.
The other answers are all beta adrenoceptor blockers. These are also drugs that we need to know about but they have no direct relevance to the alpha 1 adrenoceptor question. I will put up a separate question on the beta adrenoceptors at some point in the future. Let me know if you want me to remind you when I do this. Cheers, Alex.
best_explanation: Phenylephrine acts as an agonist on alpha 1 adrenoceptors, the others act as antagonists on beta adrenoceptors.  Alpha 1 adrenoceptors are located in smooth muscle and act to cause smooth muscle contraction, hence phenylephrine is used to test for alpha 1 adrenoceptor blockade.  Beta 2 adrenoceptors are located in the lungs and act to cause bronchodilation, hence salbutamol is used to test for beta 2 adrenoceptor activity.  Beta 1 adrenoceptors are located in the heart and act to cause heart contraction, hence isoprenaline is used to test for beta 1 adrenoceptor activity.  Alpha 2 adrenoceptors are located in the blood vessels and act to cause vasodilation, hence phenylephrine is used to test for alpha 2 adrenoceptor activity.  Alpha 3 adrenoceptors are located in the heart and act to increase heart rate, hence adrenaline is used to test for alpha 3 adrenoceptor activity.  Beta 3 adrenoceptors are located in the heart and act to decrease heart rate, hence propanolol is used to test for beta 3 adrenoceptor activity.  Note that there are different types of each class of adrenoceptors and different drugs may act on different types.  For example, beta 1 adrenoceptors can be blocked by propanolol, while beta 2 adrenoceptors can be blocked by salmeterol.  I hope this helps!  Let me know if you have any other questions.

input: Given question: Mannose & Fucose are carbohydrates found on the cell wall of bacteria. What aspect of the complement system do they activate? Option A: C3b Option B: Classical pathway Option C: Lectin pathway Option D: C3a Option E: Alternative pathway The correct answer is Option C.
reference: https://teachmephysiology.com/immune-system/innate-immune-system/complement-system/ This website explains the 3 ways in which mannose and fucose activate lectin pathway. 1) by binding to a protein on the surface of invading bacteria 2) by binding to a protein on the surface of fungi 3) by binding to a protein on the surface of viruses (not all viruses have this so not all viral infections will be detected) It also explains that once activated, a cascade occurs where C3 convertase is activated which results in downstream effects. One of these is the production of C3a and C5a which are anaphylatoxins - these stimulate mast cells and basophils to release histamine and other proinflammatory substances. Another effect is the formation of C5b which can bind to the surface of invading organisms and trigger macrophages and neutrophils to phagocytose (process of opsonisation) them.  This website is quite detailed so if you're interested in learning more, I recommend having a look! :)  Tutorial: Innate Immunity & Complement System (led by Prof Dave Wilson) & Complement System (led by Prof Graham Lord) both in Case 4. There is also a short powerpoint in the immunology folder in case 4 on the basics of the complement system. I also found the PCS unit 2 lecture on innate immunity and the complement system really helpful. Let me know if you want the link to any of those resources! :)
best_explanation: Mannose & Fucose are found on the cell wall of bacteria & when the complement system is activated, lectin pathway is activated.  C3a is the activated form of C3b which acts as an anaphylatoxin, stimulating immune response.  Alternative pathway is activated when a microbial surface component recognises a host receptor.  C3b binds to the surface of invading bacteria & fungi, making them easier for phagocytes to identify & ingest.  C3a & C5a are the anaphylatoxins which stimulate immune response. C3a binds to cell surface receptors & stimulates the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines.  C5a binds to receptors on mast cells & basophils, triggering the release of histamine, important in parasitic infections.  C5b forms part of the membrane attack complex (MAC) which punctures the target cell.  C3 is activated in 2 ways: 1) spontaneous 2) host-receptor assisted.  Only C3b is produced in the spontaneous pathway, whilst both C3b & C3a are produced in the host-receptor assisted pathway.  C3a acts as an anaphylatoxin, stimulating immune response. C3b binds to the surface of invading bacteria & fungi, making them easier for phagocytes to identify & ingest. C3b can also coat bacteria & act as an opsonin, making it easier for phagocytes to ingest.  C3 is cleaved into smaller amounts when complement is activated. These C3b fragments can join together to make a C3 convertase, which catalyses the formation of C3a & C5a.  C3a & C5a are the anaphylatoxins which stimulate immune response. C3a binds to cell surface receptors & stimulates the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines.  C5a binds to receptors on mast cells & basophils, triggering the release of histamine, important in parasitic infections.

input: Given question: The gastric phase accounts for 60% of gastric secretion. The activation of mechanoreceptors initiates the vago-vagal and local reflexes which stimulates the secretion of acetylcholine. What causes the activation of these mechanoreceptors? reference: Ghrelin is released when the stomach is empty, to stimulate the release of gastrin from the G cells. instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: What epithelial cell type functions as a mediator of filtration and diffusion? Option A: simple squamous Option B: simple cuboidal Option C: simple columnar Option D: stratified squamous Option E: pseudostratified The correct answer is Option A.
reference: simple squamous - as the name suggests, these cells are simply shaped with a single layer of cells which function as a physical barrier to prevent the passage of negatively charged ions. Simple cuboidal - function as a site of active absorption simple columnar - specialised for secretion/production of mucus/cells simple cuboidal/stratified cuboidal - sites of active absorption and secretion pseudostratified - found in the respiratory tree; each cell is connected to the basal lamina by a gap junction and the epithelium appears 'pseudostratified' because the cells are arranged at roughly equal distances from each other, giving the appearance of layers. However, each cell is actually connected to several other cells in the layer immediately beneath it. This arrangement allows for expansion/contraction without the layers themselves moving. (from microanatomy workbook answers) filtration and diffusion lecture PCS Unit 1 Little bit of extra information that might be helpful: the apical surface of simple squamous epithelial cells face the lumen of the tubule/duct whereas the basal surface is attached to the basement membrane. The lateral surfaces are free to move and can contract/expand To allow for diffusion to occur, specific transporters must be present on the plasma membrane. For example, Na+/K+ ATPase pump will remove Na+ after it has been filtered into the tubule/duct and K+ will diffuse back into the cell down its concentration gradient. Na+ will then diffuse back into the cell when it's concentration is higher on the outside. (Diffusion lecture PCS unit 1) also the following video is very helpful and easy to understand: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CMZ2AormwgU (10 mins)
best_explanation: simple squamous - as the name suggests, these cells are just one layer thick and are found in locations where filtration and diffusion are the main functions. simple cuboidal - these are two or three layered cuboidal shaped cells. They produce secretions that are released into ducts. simple columnar - these cells are shaped like a column and can be classified into two types. Type 1 - the cell has multiple microvilli and the nucleus is always pushed to one side. Type 2 - the nucleus is in the centre of the cell. They are found in the small intestine and form the secretions of digestive enzymes and bicarbonate. pseudostratified - these cells are layered like a stratum, but the layers are not tightly bound. They are found in the respiratory and digestive tracts. stratified squamous - these cells are found in locations where there is a high risk of abrasion. They are found in the epididymis and the vagina.  In summary, simple squamous cells are the epithelial cells which function as a mediator of filtration and diffusion. Simple columnar cells are found in the small intestine and form the secretions of digestive enzymes and bicarbonate. Pseudostratified epithelium is found in the respiratory and digestive tracts. Stratified squamous epithelium is found in the epididymis and the vagina. Simple cuboidal epithelium is found in locations where the cells produce secretions that are released into ducts. input: Given question: Jim's just gotten a new iPhone and is playing around with portrait mode on the camera app. The way the camera is able to focus on a nearby object and blur out objects in the distance reminds him of how the human eye works in a similar way. The ciliary muscle in the eye controls accommodation for viewing objects at varying distances. Which cranial nerve innervates this muscle? Option A: Ophthalmic nerve (branch of CN V trigeminal nerve) Option B: Optic nerve (CN II) Option C: Oculomotor nerve (CN III) Option D: Abducens nerve (CN VI) Option E: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) The correct answer is Option C.
reference: C is correct! The oculomotor nerve supplies motor function to the superior, inferior and medial rectus (the 3 main 'muscles' of the eyeball), as well as parasympathetic innervation to the ciliary muscle (which controls accommodation), and the levator palebrae (which acts to close the eyelids).  A - although the ophthalmic nerve (a branch of the trigeminal CN V) does have sensory innervation to the cornea, it doesn't actually supply any motor function to the eye itself. B - Although the optic nerve does receive visual information from the retina, it doesn't actually control any muscles within the eye itself.D & E - These two nerves don't even innervate any parts of the eye at all! D is quite tricky as the abducens nerve does give motor innervation to the lateral rectus muscle of the eyeball, but C is still more correct as it also gives parasympathetic innervation to the ciliary muscle. E - The trochlear nerve only has motor innervation to one muscle - the superior oblique muscle of the eyeball, but while this is technically correct, it's not as accurate as C which covers both the ciliary muscle AND the levator palpebrae.
best_explanation:
C is correct! The oculomotor nerve supplies motor function to the superior, inferior and medial rectus and inferior oblique muscles as well as the ciliary muscle which controls accommodation.  The optic nerve carries visual information from the retina. The ophthalmic nerve (a branch of the trigeminal CN V) supplies sensory information from the cornea and conjunctiva. The abducens nerve (CN VI) supplies the lateral rectus muscle which abducts the eye and the trochlear nerve (CN IV) supplies the superior oblique muscle which effects superior and inferior rotations of the eye. input: Given question: Calcinosis is the calcification of soft tissues ( including kidneys,heart , lungs etc) What vitamin could cause this if it is ingested in excess? Option A: A Option B: B6 Option C: B9 Option D: D The correct answer is Option D.
reference: Vitamin D, when ingested in excess can causecalcinosis. This can occur through a few different mechanisms. One is that it causes increased absorption of calcium, and so more calcium is laid down in soft tissues. Another is that it inhibits the function of 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferal (the activated from of vitamin D) which is responsible for promoting bone health and reducing calcium levels in the blood. This means that more calcium is released from bones and into the blood, where it can be deposited in soft tissues such as the kidneys and heart.  Too much vitamin A can also cause calcinosis, but this is far less common.  Too much vitamin D is most commonly encountered as a result of sun worshipping or using sunbeds.  Symptoms of vitamin D toxicity include; vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion, cardiac arrhythmias and in severe cases renal failure.  It is rare to get vitamin D toxicity through just dietary intake, however, it is possible if one were to consume large amounts of foods that are fortified with vitamin D (e.g. cereal, milk and orange juice), or if one takes a lot of supplements containing vitamin D.  It is important to note that many people do not ingest enough vitamin D, and so may develop rickets (a disease that affects bone development) as a result.  I hope this helps! Let me know if you have any other questions.
best_explanation: Vitamin D if ingested in excess can cause calcinosis. This is because vitamin D is a precursor for calcitriol which causes calcium to be released from the bones and also inhibits its reabsorption. As vitamin D is fat soluble it can be stored in fatty tissues for later use. This means that it is possible to ingest excess vitamin D.  Vitamin A can also cause calcinosis but this is more likely to be due to a deficiency in vitamin D as vitamin A can cause vitamin D deficiency. This is because vitamin A is able to compete with vitamin D for the same binding sites on the bone.  B6 and B9 deficiencies are unlikely to cause calcinosis.  B6 deficiency may cause a reduced activity of the enzymes involved in the synthesis of neurotransmitters and so can cause neurological problems.  B9 deficiency can cause a reduction in RBC production and so can cause anaemia.  http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/vitamin-d-excess-and-vitamin-d-deficiency  http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/vitamin-b6-deficiency  http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/vitamin-b9-deficiency  http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/anemia-and-red-blood-cell-disorders  http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/neurological-disorders-and-conditions  ( These websites are very useful for looking up the effects of vitamin deficiencies and excess )  Hope this helps. input: Given question: A 77 year old man visits the GPs surgery. His history states he has genetic haemochromatosis. What mineral is causing his condition? Option A: Phosphorus Option B: Iron Option C: Iodine Option D: Copper Option E: Calcium The correct answer is Option B.
reference: Haemochromatosis is the accumulation of iron in the body leading to iron overload. The HFE gene controls the amount of iron absorbed by the intestine. Mutations in this gene cause a hereditary form of haemochromatosis. best_explanation: The correct answer is D - the patient is experiencing respiratory alkalosis secondary to hyperventilation. input: Given question: During inflammation, neutrophils migrate to the site of injury. There are three steps to neutrophil migration: Rolling, Adhesion and Transmigration. Each of these phases requires proteins to help them occur, which of the following proteins is essential in the rolling phase of neutrophil migration? Option A: Selectins Option B: Integrins Option C: PECAM-1 Option D: Fibrin Option E: Keratin The correct answer is Option A.
reference:
Selectins are carbohydrate binding molecules (CBMs) that are expressed on the endothelial wall. They mediate the rolling of neutrophils along the endothelium. Integrins are involved in firm adhesion of the neutrophil to the endothelium. PECAM-1 (CD31) is a protein involved in the transmigration phase. It acts as a bridge for neutrophils to cross the endothelium. Fibrin is a protein involved in the platelet plug formation. It is laid down by the platelets after they have come to rest on the subendothelial surface. Keratin is a structural protein found in the cytoskeleton of mammalian epithelial cells. It is not involved in neutrophil migration. Information source: https://teachmephysiology.com/immune-system/innate-immune-system/inflammation/neutrophil-migration/ Rolling: selectins are involvedAdhesion: integrins are involvedTransmigration: PECAM-1 is involved Other important molecules involved in inflammation:TNF-alpha: causes vasodilation and increases phagocytosisC5a: increases phagocytosisIL-1: causes local vasodilation and increases phagocytosisIL-8: causes neutrophil attraction IL-6: causes local tissue destruction and counter immunityReference: Applied immunology and microbiology post tutorial document. best_explanation: Selectins are carbohydrate-binding proteins that are expressed on the neutrophil's surface. They bind to carbohydrates expressed on the endothelium, allowing the neutrophil to "roll" along the endothelium. Integrins are involved in firm adhesion of the neutrophil to the endothelium. PECAM-1 is an adhesion molecule expressed on the endothelium that interacts with integrins on the neutrophil. Fibrin is a protein which is part of the clotting cascade, it is not involved in neutrophil migration. Keratin is a structural protein found in the nucleus of cells, it is not involved in neutrophil migration. https://teachmephysiology.com/immune-system/innate-immune-system/inflammation/neutrophil-migration/ Rolling: Selectins on the neutrophil bind to carbohydrates (such as mucin) expressed on the endothelium. The neutrophil can now "roll" along the endothelium. Adhesion: Integrins on the neutrophil bind to PECAM-1 on the endothelium. Transmigration: The neutrophil now sits firmly on the endothelium and extrudes its contents, including neutrophil elastase, into the tissues. It also gets "pushed" through the endothelium by the redistribution of the cytoskeleton. input: Given question: You are shadowing an eye surgeon and he suddenly turns to you and asks, 'WHAT TYPE OF COLLAGEN IS FOUND IN THE CORNEA!!!!'. You are caught off-guard and can't quite remember what type. What type of collagen is found in the cornea? Option A: Type I Option B: Type II Option C: Type III Option D: Type IV Option E: Type V The correct answer is Option A.
reference:
The cornea is made up of Type I collagen. This is the same as scar tissue and bone. It is a structural collagen. There are 3 main layers to the cornea - epithelium, Bowman's membrane (Type IV collagen) and stroma (Type I collagen). The stroma is the thickest layer and is made almost entirely of Type I collagen. This gives the cornea it's strength. In addition, there are also nerve endings, blood vessels and macrophages present in the stroma. The cornea has a very high oxygen concentration which is important in preventing infection by reducing the numbers of microorganisms that can survive. The cornea also contains some keratan sulfate and chondroitin sulfate. These give the cornea additional strength and help to prevent dehydration. The epithelium is composed of multiple layers of cells which are held together by desmosine and laminine. The most important cell in the epithelium is the corneal keratocyte. It is believed that these cells are responsible for creating new corneas in case of damage. Finally, the Bowman's membrane is a thin layer of collagen that separates the cornea from the sclera. It is named after its discoverer, Sir William Bowman. It is thought that this layer may help to even out any irregularities in the surface of the cornea so that the light is not distorted as it enters the eye. If there is damage to the cornea, the body produces new collagen for the Bowman's membrane to repair it.  Adapted from PCS Unit 1 - The Cornea and Conjunctiva lecture.
