I hope you find this helpful :)  Disclaimer: I am not a medical professional so this information should not be used to diagnose or treat any conditions. It is just general knowledge that I have learnt and wanted to share :)
best_explanation: The cornea is made up of type I collagen. The cornea has a high refractive index so helps to focus the light as it enters the eye. It also has a large number of keratocytes which are loose connective tissue cells that support the shape of the cornea. The stroma of the cornea is made up of more collagen (Type I) and less keratocytes. This is so the stroma is more transparent and less likely to scatter light.  Link to learning outcome:  From 'Tissue Engineering and Bioprocessing' learning outcome 1. Understand the biology of the eye and its associated diseases.  More information:  The cornea is a key part of the eye, it is the clear outer layer at the front of the eye. The cornea has a very high refractive index, and so helps to focus the light as it enters the eye. The cornea is also very transparent, and so allows most of the light to pass through it. The cornea is made up of five layers, from top to bottom they are: 1. Epithelium2. Bowman's membrane3. Stroma4. Descemet's membrane5. Endothelium The epithelium is a simple squamous epithelium, which is non-ciliated and secretes a layer of mucus. The bowman's membrane is a thin layer of collagen that separates the cornea from the sclera. The stroma is the thickest part of the cornea, and is made up of 90% collagen (Type I) and 10% keratocytes. The stroma is transparent to allow light to pass through. The descemet's membrane is a thin layer of collagen that separates the stroma from the endothelium. The endothelium is a simple squamous epithelium, but it is ciliated. The cilia help to keep the cornea clear of debris.  For more information on the cornea, here is a useful link: https://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/cornea-and-conjunctiva. input: Given question: Which of the following imaging methods does not use ionising radiation? Option A: CT scan Option B: Fluoroscopy Option C: MRI Option D: PET scan Option E: X-rays The correct answer is Option C.
reference: CT scans - uses ionising radiation (X-rays) to produce detailed images of the body's tissues and organs. They are often used to diagnose problems such as tumours, cysts, fractures and infections.  Fluoroscopy - uses ionising radiation (X-rays) to produce real-time moving images of the inside of the body. It is often used to guide procedures such as injections or biopsies.  PET scans - also uses ionising radiation (positron emission tomography) to produce detailed images of the body's tissues and organs. However, they work by detecting the gamma rays emitted by a tracer substance (such as glucose) rather than by exposure to X-rays directly.  X-rays - non-invasive diagnostic test that uses ionising radiation to produce images of the body's tissues and organs. They are commonly used to diagnose conditions of the bones, joints, heart, lungs and digestive system.  MRI - does not expose the body to ionising radiation. Instead, it uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to produce detailed images of the body's tissues and organs.  Ultrasound - also does not expose the body to ionising radiation. Instead, it uses high frequency sound waves to produce images of the body's tissues and organs. It is commonly used during pregnancy to check on the development of the foetus. Fluoroscopy uses ionising radiation (x-rays) to produce real-time moving images of the body. It is often used to guide procedures such as injections and biopsies. Option A: The isthmus of the uterine tube Option B: The fimbrae of the uterine tube Option C: The infundibulum of the uterine tube Option D: The ampulla of the uterine tube Option E: The intramural area of the uterine tube The correct answer is Option D.
reference: The ampulla is the curved portion at the end of the uterine tube, opposite the fimbrae. This is where fertilisation usually occurs. If fertilisation does not occur here, the zygote will travel into the infundibulum. The infundibulum is the straight portion leading to the uterus. Here, the zygote will either be absorbed or enter the uterus. If it enters the uterus, it will implant in the lining (endometrium) and grow into a foetus. The isthmus is the narrowest part of the uterine tube, just before the fimbrae. The fimbrae are the hair-like projections that help catch and direct the ovum. The intralmural area is the area within the muscular walls of the uterus. Most blastocytes (8 day old embryos) will travel here if they are not fertilised in the ampulla. Some may be able to develop into blastocysts but most will be absorbed by the endometrium. input: Given question: A slow of prolonged depolarization is known as accommodation, this may result in an increase in the threshold potential. What may be the possible cause of this prolonged depolarization? Option A: Sodium- potassium pump ceases to work Option B: inactivation of potassium ion voltage gated channel Option C: Inactivation of sodium ion voltage gated channel Option D: activation  of potassium voltage gated channel Option E: activation of Calcium ion voltage gated channel The correct answer is Option C.
reference: when the voltage gated sodium channels are inactivated it will take longer for the action potential to repolarize and the membrane potential will become more negative. This is known as depolarization rescue. If the sodium channels remain inactivated for a prolonged period it can lead to an increase in the threshold potential.  The other answers and their corresponding mechanism are: A; when the Na+K+ pump ceases to work sodium concentration gradient across the cell membrane falls resulting in a decrease in the rate of depolarization.  B; when the potassium ion channels are inactivated the membrane becomes more difficult to depolarize.  D; When the potassium channels are activated this increases the rate of repolarization.E; when calcium channels are activated it results in sustained depolarization which leads to increased entry of sodium ions due to the voltage gate being open for longer leading to increased rate of depolarization.
best_explanation: A slow of prolonged depolarization is known as accommodation, this may result in an increase in the threshold potential. The possible cause of this prolonged depolarization is the inactivation of the sodium ion voltage gated channel. He presents with numbness in the thenar eminence of his palm in addition to pain and tingling in his thumb and lateral two and a half fingers. reference: https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/nerves/median-nerve/carpal-tunnel/ - clinical relevance box at bottomCarpal tunnel syndrome occurs when there is entrapment of the median nerve as it travels through the wrist at the carpal tunnel. This causes pain, numbness and tingling in the hand. It can be caused by anything that reduces the size of the carpal tunnel (eg oedema). In this case, the thenar eminence (located on the anterior surface of the palm) is also affected because the median nerve supplies the flexors of the hand (including the flexor pollicis longus which flexes the thumb at the MCP joint). Therefore, weakness of the thenar eminence (ie poor grip) is common. There are several ways to treat carpal tunnel syndrome (non-surgical and surgical) but the most important thing is to identify and address any underlying cause (eg diabetes, obesity). Symptoms include pain, tingling and numbness in the median side of the hand (thumb and lateral two and a half fingers).In this case, the thenar eminence is also affected due to the fact that the median nerve supplies the thenar muscles.Muscles of the hand innervated by the ulnar nerve (ulnar side of the hand) are unaffected by carpal tunnel syndrome.Therefore, the numbness in the thenar eminence, pain and tingling in the thumb and lateral 2.5 fingers are all consistent with a diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome. input: Given question: "This type of bone is typically found in areas of the body where extensive organ protection is required." Which type of bone does this statement best fit? Option A: Flat bone Option B: Long bone Option C: Sesamoid bone Option D: Short bone Option E: Sutural bone The correct answer is Option A.
reference:
This would be a flat bone as flat bones are typically found in areas of extensive organ protection, such as the skull and ribs. Examples of flat bones include the scapula, pelvis and sacrum. Long bones are typically found in the limbs and are used for locomotion. Examples of long bones include the tibia and fibula, and the humerus and radius.Short bones are smaller bones that do not have a shaft. They are often found between other bones or near joints. An example of a short bone would be the phalanges in your fingers.Sesamoid bones are bones embedded in tendons. These small, round bones are commonly found in the tendons of the hands, knees, and feet. An example of a sesamoid bone would be the patella, which is embedded in the tendon of the quadriceps femoris muscle.Sutural bones are, technically speaking, sesamoid bones, but they are classified separately because they are so small. Sutural bones are found in the walls of the middle ear, in the foramen ovale (a hole in the side of the skull), and in the nasal cavity.An example of sutural bones would be the ossicles of the ear - the malleus, incus and stapes. The ossicular chain is connected to the eardrum by a series of small, boneless joints called sutures. The ossicles themselves are sesamoid bones, embedded in the tendon of the tympanic membrane. (Teach me Anatomy)Flat bone - typically found in areas of extensive organ protectionLong bone - typically found in the limbs for locomotionShort bone - smaller bones between other bones or near jointsSesamoid bone - bones embedded in tendonsSutural bone - similar to sesamoid bones but classified separately due to size For more information on bones, I found Teach Me Anatomy incredibly helpful (and it's free!). It has a lot of easy to understand information on all aspects of anatomy. https://teachmeanatomy.info/the-basics/classification/bone-classification/ (I hope this helps!)
I'm sorry, I didn't mean to copy and paste everything from the website! I just wanted to use some examples to help explain the question. I'll delete it if you let me know. Thank you.
best_explanation:
Flat bones are typically found in areas of the body where extensive organ protection is required. For example, the ribs protect the lungs, and the pelvis protects the abdominal organs.  Long bones are the bones of the limbs and are principally responsible for supporting the body's weight.  Sesamoid bones are bones embedded in tendons. These small, round bones are commonly found in the tendons of the hands, knees, and feet.  Short bones are bones that are commonly found in the hands and feet.  Sutural bones, also called wormian bones, are the small bones found in the sutures of the skull.  As a reminder, a bone's main structural function is to support and protect the soft tissues such as muscles, tendons, and organs.  Hope this helps. Let me know if you have any other questions. instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Which one of the following cells in the lung parenchyma produces surfactant? Option A: Alveolar macrophage Option B: Endothelial cell Option C: Type I pneumocyte Option D: Goblet cell Option E: Type II pneumocyte The correct answer is Option E.
reference: Type II pneumocytes produce a large amount of surfactant and are found in the lung interstitium. When they die, their membranes break down to form lipid-rich vacuoles which are taken up by adjacent type II pneumocytes. This is how surfactant is recycled. Alveolar macrophages engulf dead red blood cells and other structures that have breached the alveoli.Endothelial cells line the blood vessels of the lungs.Goblet cells produce mucus which is stored in their rough endoplasmic reticulum. If stimulated, they will secrete mucus into the alveoli where it traps pathogens.  Type I pneumocytes are found in the lung interstitium and are thought to be relatively inert. However, they can be activated by the release of tumour necrosis factor alpha from monocytes in response to infection. They then become cytotoxic and produce reactive oxygen species.  Adapted from Pocock & Richards - page 698 (2013) "The lung interstitium: lung cells and their functions" http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441980/#:~:text=Type%20I%20pneumocytes%20are%20relatively,activated%20by%20the%20release%20of%20TNF%20alpha.&text=Goblet%20cells%20store%20mucus,%20secrete,alveoli%20where%20it%20traps%20pathogens.&text=Endothelial%20cells%20line%20the%20blood%20vessels,of%20the%20lungs.&text=Alveolar%20macrophages%20engulf%20dead%20red%20blood%20cells,and%20other%20structures%20that%20have%20breached%20the%20alveoli.%2C(adapted%20from%20Pocock%20&%20Richards%20-%20page%20698%20(2013)%20"The%20lung%20interstitium:%20lung%20cells%20and%20their%20functions"%20http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441980/#:~:text=Type%20I%20pneumocytes%20are%20relatively,activated%20by%20the%20release%20of%20TNF%20alpha.&text=Goblet%20cells%20store%20mucus,%20secrete,alveoli%20where%20it%20traps%20pathogens.&text=Endothelial%20cells%20line%20the%20blood%20vessels,of%20the%20lungs.&text=Alveolar%20macrophages%20engulf%20dead%20red%20blood%20cells,%20and%20other%20structures%20that%20have%20breached%20the%20alveoli.%2C(adapted%20from%20Pocock%20&%20Richards%20-%20page%20698%20(2013)%20"The%20lung%20interstitium:%20lung%20cells%20and%20their%20functions"%20http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441980/#:~:text=Type%20I%20pneumocytes%20are%20relatively,activated%20by%20the%20release%20of%20TNF%20alpha.&text=Goblet%20cells%20store
best_explanation: Type II pneumocytes produce surfactant and are the only cells in the lung parenchyma that do so.  Alveolar macrophages, endothelial cells, goblet cells and type I pneumocytes do not produce surfactant.  Alveolar macrophages are cells of the innate immune system that reside in the lung interstitium.  Endothelial cells line the alveoli and form the blood-air barrier.  Goblet cells produce mucus which is stored in the acini.  Type I pneumocytes are the cells in the lung interstitium that produce collagen.  Surfactant is composed of phospholipids combined with carbohydrates and proteins, produced by type II pneumocytes. It lowers the surface tension of water, allowing the alveoli to expand properly.  The alveoli would collapse in the absence of surfactant.  The presence of surfactant makes the alveoli more stable and less prone to collapse.
